{{Legend0|#999999|Independent hold}} | title = [[Speaker of the United States House of Representatives|Speaker]] | before_election = [[Newt Gingrich]] | before_party = Republican Party (US) | after_election = [[Dennis Hastert]] | after_party = Republican Party (US) }} The '''1998 United States House of Representatives elections''' were held on November 3, 1998, to elect [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. Representatives]] to serve in the [[106th United States Congress]]. They were part of the [[midterm elections]] held during [[President of the United States|President]] [[Bill Clinton]]'s second term. They were a major disappointment for the Republicans, who were expecting to gain seats due to the embarrassment Clinton suffered during the [[Monica Lewinsky scandal]] and the "[[six-year itch]]" effect observed in most second-term midterm elections. However, the Republicans lost five seats to the Democrats, although they retained a narrow majority in the House. A wave of Republican discontent with Speaker [[Newt Gingrich]] prompted him to resign shortly after the election; he was replaced by Congressman [[Dennis Hastert]] of Illinois. The campaign was marked by Republican attacks on the morality of President [[Bill Clinton]], with independent counsel [[Kenneth Starr]] having released his report on the Lewinsky scandal and House leaders having initiated [[Impeachment inquiry into Bill Clinton|an inquiry]] into whether [[Federal impeachment in the United States|impeachable]] offenses had occurred. However, exit polls indicated that most voters opposed impeaching Clinton, and predictions of high Republican or low Democratic turnout due to the scandal failed to materialize.{{Cite web |title=Election '98 Lewinsky factor never materialized - November 4, 1998 |url=http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/stories/1998/11/04/impeachment/index.html |website=www.cnn.com}} Some speculate that the losses reflected a backlash against the Republicans for attacking the popular Clinton. With the Republicans having lost four House seats and failing to gain any seats in the Senate, it was the first time since [[1934 United States House of Representatives elections|1934]] that the non-presidential party failed to gain congressional seats in a midterm election; this would happen again in [[2002 United States House of Representatives elections|2002]]. This was the last election until [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections|2024]] where no incumbents who served at least 6 terms (12 years) lost re-nomination or re-election, and it was also the most recent where no Democratic incumbent lost renomination.See {{Cite web |last=Singer |first=Jeff |date=April 21, 2014 |title=We Unlucky Few: A Look at the Incumbents Who Lost Their Primaries, 1994-2012 |url=https://www.dailykos.com/stories/2014/4/20/1264682/-We-unlucky-few-A-look-at-the-incumbents-who-lost-their-primaries-1994-2012#comment_53204306 |website=Daily Kos}} == Results == === Federal === {| style="width:60%; text-align:center" |+ ↓ |- style="color:white" | style="background:{{party color|Democratic Party (US)}}; width:48.51%" | '''211''' | style="background:{{party color|Independent}}; width:0.23%" | '''1''' | style="background:{{party color|Republican Party (US)}}; width:51.26%" | '''223''' |- | '''Democratic''' | '''I''' | '''Republican''' |} {| class=wikitable style="text-align:center" |- valign=bottom ! rowspan=2 colspan=2 | Party ! colspan=3 | Seats ! rowspan=2 | Seat
